result:
I sometimes imagine a museum devoted entirely to ordinary things that almost nobody thought to save. Not crowns, not swords, not the first machine to accomplish something spectacular. A museum of grocery lists, worn doormats, refrigerator magnets, and the little plastic clips that keep bread bags closed. Its purpose would be modest: to remind visitors that most of human life happened somewhere other than the places where history was officially being made.

The entrance would be easy to miss. Perhaps it would occupy a former hardware store, with the old lettering still visible above the windows. Admission would cost whatever you could spare. Behind the counter, an attendant would be repairing a stapler rather than looking at a screen. There would be no dramatic introductory film. You would simply step inside and find, in the first glass case, a key whose lock no longer exists.

That key would deserve a proper label.

“Brass. Date uncertain. Carried for approximately nineteen years. Opened a back door.”

Below this, in smaller print, the museum might explain that the owner continued carrying it for several months after moving away. Nobody knows why. Forgetfulness is possible. So is reluctance. Sometimes the hand understands that a chapter has ended before the heart does, and sometimes it is the other way around.

A whole gallery could be given over to objects that outlived their usefulness without losing their authority. The remote control for a discarded television. A charger belonging to an unidentified device. A button in a sewing tin, kept because its matching coat might still be somewhere. These things occupy drawers in millions of homes, awaiting a reunion that becomes less likely every year. Throwing them away would require someone to abandon the search.

Another room would contain recorded household sounds. The particular cough of an old refrigerator starting up. Radiator pipes knocking at midnight. A screen door slamming two houses down. Someone washing dishes while someone else, in another room, practices the same difficult passage on a piano. Visitors would sit on mismatched chairs and listen through headphones. Occasionally, a person would begin crying without being able to explain which sound had done it.

We tend to imagine memory as a collection of pictures. Yet a place can return through the ears with extraordinary force. A certain engine noise restores the back seat of a childhood car. The rattle of cutlery brings back a kitchen, including its light, its temperature, and the person standing at the sink. You might have forgotten the wallpaper entirely until a spoon strikes a bowl at just the right pitch.

The museum would be careful about its labels. Curators, like everyone else, can be tempted to make a good story better. Beside a chipped blue mug, there might be a note admitting that its owner could not remember where she bought it. She remembered only that she preferred it to her other mugs and became annoyed when guests chose it. That would be enough to earn the mug its place on the shelf.

I would want an exhibit about repairs. A sock darned with thread of the wrong color. A chair reinforced by someone who understood stability better than elegance. A cookbook held together with tape, its most frequently consulted page translucent with butter. Such objects make the work of keeping things visible. You can see where a knee pressed through fabric, where a chair leg loosened, where a hand repeatedly turned a page.

Nearby, perhaps, would be a workbench where visitors could bring something broken. The museum would employ patient people with excellent lamps. They could not promise to fix everything. A radio might remain silent; a cracked plate might be suitable only for display. Still, visitors could watch someone examine an object closely before deciding it was finished. Children would be welcome to ask questions, provided they kept their fingers away from the soldering iron.

There should also be room for ordinary failures. A notebook abandoned after six enthusiastic pages. Running shoes worn twice. A phrasebook purchased before a trip that never happened. These would need no cautionary captions about discipline. The notebook’s owner might have found a different occupation, or become ill, or simply discovered that she disliked keeping a diary. Visitors could supply their own explanations, preferably more than one, before moving along.

In the center of the building, I imagine a large table covered with grocery lists. They would be arranged by no particular hierarchy: hurried pencil beside careful ink, expensive ingredients beside potatoes and soap. Some would contain calculations in the margins. Others would include messages: “Call when you get there.” “Something for dinner.” “The kind Dad likes.” A list might end with a single emphatic word, underlined twice: “Coffee.”

School groups would probably enjoy the telephones most. The children would lift receivers, turn dials, and wonder how anyone tolerated waiting for the numbers to come back around. Their teachers would explain busy signals. Someone would ask what happened if you called a house and nobody was home. For a moment, the adults might struggle to make the answer sound plausible. You hung up. Later, if you remembered, you tried again.

The final gallery would be almost empty. It would contain a table, a lamp, and a stack of blank cards. A sign would ask visitors to describe an ordinary object they wished they still had. People might write about a father’s gardening gloves or a cheap watch worn through their first years away from home. Others would struggle to describe something whose appearance had faded, though they could still remember its weight.

Before leaving, you could pin your card to the wall or take it home. Then you would retrieve your coat, check your pockets, and step out through the former hardware store’s door. Nothing outside would have changed very much. A delivery driver would be looking for an address. Someone would be sweeping a shop entrance. At home, your own cup would be waiting beside the sink, with a little tea drying in the bottom. You would wash it, perhaps noticing the small chip near its handle, and put it back in the cupboard where it belonged.
